title: Rā' II — the sākin cases, the five istiʿlāʾ words, and where both readings are allowed
objectives: Student can state the sākin rule in one line — a sākin rā' takes its ruling from the vowel BEFORE it — and apply it on sight.
Student can say why the kasra of a hamzat waṣl does not count, and read ٱرْجِعِىٓ heavy.
Student can recognise the five istiʿlāʾ exception words on sight, and knows she is not expected to derive them.
Student can say why ٱلْقَدْرِ is light in waṣl and heavy at waqf, decide before she reads which one she is doing, and name the three cases where both readings are transmitted.

slides.heading: Lesson 3.10 — Rā' II: sākin cases, the five words, and jawāz al-wajhayn
Two words on the board, and only one of them is heavy
body: Write وَٱسْتَغْفِرْهُ (110:3) and قِرْطَاسٍ (6:7) side by side. Both have a sākin rā'. Both have a kasra before it. Both have a heavy letter somewhere in the word. One is light and one is heavy — and if she reads them both the same way, whichever way, one of them is wrong.
Then name the error before it happens, because it is the one that actually occurs: she will read وَٱسْتَغْفِرْهُ heavy, because of the غ.
And the غ is a red herring. It comes BEFORE the rā'. Only a FOLLOWING istiʿlāʾ letter counts. That single fact is the difference between the two words on the board.

Then the third thing, which is the real content of the lesson and should be said as a warning: this is the lesson where students start deriving. Do not. Condition 6 fires in exactly five words in the entire Qur'an. Learn to recognise five words and move on — nobody needs to derive this.

Take her answer to last session's homework question first: in صُدُورِ, why is the ر light when the ص right before it is heavy? Because the rā' has its own vowel, and a rā' with its own vowel looks nowhere else. Today is what happens when it has no vowel of its own.

audio.cue: 110:3 — a sākin rā' after an ORIGINAL kasra, so LIGHT. There is a heavy غ in the word and it is on the wrong side. Point at the page: which side of the rā' is the heavy letter on?
6:7 — reference example, outside your memorized surahs. Sākin rā' after a kasra, but a ط FOLLOWS it in the same word, so the rā' is dragged HEAVY. One of exactly five words.

slides.heading: The new baseline, written next to last lesson's
body: A sākin rā' takes its ruling from the vowel BEFORE it. Fatḥa before it → heavy. Ḍamma before it → heavy. Kasra before it → light, with two qualifiers that are coming next.

Then the whole family in two sentences, and she should be able to say both from memory by the end of the unit. A VOWELLED rā' takes its ruling from its own vowel. A SĀKIN rā' takes its ruling from the vowel before it. Everything else is qualification.

Drill the plain cases before touching a qualifier. تَرْمِيهِم (105:4) — fatḥa before the ر — heavy. وَأَرْسَلَ (105:3) — fatḥa — heavy. ٱلْقُرْءَانُ (2:185) — ḍamma — heavy. وَٱسْتَغْفِرْهُ (110:3) — kasra — LIGHT.
Three of those four are in surahs she is memorising or has memorised. Lead from them rather than from the reference example.

وَٱسْتَغْفِرْهُ is the one to spend time on. There is a غ in the word — an istiʿlāʾ letter, unmistakably heavy — and the rā' is still light, because the غ comes before the ر. It is in Sūrat an-Naṣr, three ayat long, which she will memorise later in this unit. It is the single best light-sākin-rā' she has in range, and the غ makes it a trap. Drill it more than the rest.

Lesson 3-03 gave her خُصَّ ضَغْطٍ قِظْ, and today is where that set does its most conspicuous work. Every one of the five exception words is an exception BECAUSE an istiʿlāʾ letter follows the rā'. If the seven letters are not automatic, this lesson will not stick — check them in the first two minutes.

audio.cue: 105:4 — fatḥa before the sākin rā'. HEAVY. Say the vowel out loud before you read the word.
2:185 — reference example, outside your memorized surahs. Ḍamma before the sākin rā'. HEAVY.

slides.heading: Drill 1 — the two lines, and Drill 2 — plain sākin cases
slides.instructions: Drill 1, every session, out loud, before anything else: 'A vowelled rā' takes its own vowel. A sākin rā' takes the vowel before it.' Drill 2: say the vowel BEFORE the rā' out loud, then read the word. Naming the vowel first is what stops her guessing from the sound.

audio.cue: 110:3 — kasra → LIGHT. And the غ is on the wrong side.
89:10 — reference example, outside your memorized surahs. Original kasra → LIGHT.
18:107 — reference example, outside your memorized surahs. Original kasra → LIGHT.

slides.heading: Qualifier 1 — the kasra must be ORIGINAL
body: A kasra that only exists because of a hamzat al-waṣl does not count. It is a connecting vowel: it is there when you begin on the word, and it vanishes the instant you join to the word before. It was never the rā's own.
ٱرْجِعِىٓ (89:28) — HEAVY, not light. Reference example, outside your memorized surahs.
Give her the test as a sentence: 'If I join this word to the one before it, does the kasra survive?' If it disappears, ignore it.

Lesson 2-09 taught her hamzat al-waṣl — the connecting hamzah that is pronounced when you begin on a word and vanishes when you join to it. Today that fact becomes a ruling: a kasra that disappears when you join was never really the rā's.
This is a small class of words and she does not need to hunt for them. What she needs is to not be surprised when one turns up.
Flag it now for next session, because it reverses: for the lām of the Divine Name, EVERY kasra counts, including connecting ones. Two rules, two answers, and she should not try to unify them.

audio.cue: 89:28 — reference example, outside your memorized surahs. The kasra you can see belongs to a hamzat waṣl. Join the word to the one before it and watch the kasra go. HEAVY.
89:10 — reference example, outside your memorized surahs. Here the kasra is the ف's own and survives joining. LIGHT. The contrast pair for ٱرْجِعِىٓ.

slides.heading: Qualifier 2 — the five istiʿlāʾ words, given as a card and not as a derivation
body: The rule: a sākin rā' after an ORIGINAL kasra is light UNLESS a ḥarf istiʿlāʾ follows it IN THE SAME WORD — in which case the heavy letter pulls the rā' heavy.

This fires in exactly five words in the whole Qur'an. قِرْطَاسٍ, 6:7, with a ط. وَإِرْصَادًا, 9:107, with a ص. فِرْقَةٍ, 9:122, with a ق. مِرْصَادًا, 78:21, with a ص. لَبِٱلْمِرْصَادِ, 89:14, with a ص.

All five lie OUTSIDE the surahs she is memorising. These are reference examples — outside your memorized surahs — not hifz. Say that plainly, in those words. She should be able to RECOGNISE them if one appears on a page; she is not banking them, she is not hunting for them, and she is not deriving them.

Then say why the list is closed and worth trusting: do not extend it by analogy. Any sākin rā' after an original kasra with a heavy letter somewhere later in the word is NOT automatically on this list. It is five words. Recognise, do not derive.

Two performance notes. The alif after a heavy rā' is heavy — قِرْطَاسٍ, مِرْصَادًا — which is lesson 3-07's rule, unchanged. And the istiʿlāʾ letter must follow in the SAME word: a heavy letter at the start of the next word does not reach back.

The physical reason, if she wants one: the tongue has to still be raised at the moment it makes the rā'. A heavy letter that has already been and gone does not keep it raised, because the letters in between have brought it down. A heavy letter that is coming next has the tongue already rising while the rā' is being made.

audio.cue: 6:7 — reference example, outside your memorized surahs. Exception 1 of 5. The ط follows the rā'. Heavy rā', and the alif after it is heavy too.
9:107 — reference example, outside your memorized surahs. Exception 2 of 5. The ص follows the rā'. In the muṣḥaf the word carries a prefixed wāw.
9:122 — reference example, outside your memorized surahs. Exception 3 of 5. The ق follows the rā', and it carries a sukūn.
78:21 — reference example, outside your memorized surahs. Exception 4 of 5. The ص follows, and the alif after the ص is heavy.
89:14 — reference example, outside your memorized surahs. Exception 5 of 5. The ص follows. Same root as the fourth, and both are on the card.

slides.heading: Drill 3 — which side is the heavy letter on, and Drill 4 — the five-word card
slides.instructions: Drill 3: for each word, POINT at the istiʿlāʾ letter on the page and say 'before' or 'after' before you give the ruling. Pointing rather than answering from memory is the whole drill. Drill 4: read the card twice a day. Do not derive it and do not extend it. Then say the sixth-that-isn't.

audio.cue: 89:10 — no istiʿlāʾ letter at all. Light.
26:63 — reference example, outside your memorized surahs. The sixth that is NOT. Both readings transmitted; tarqīq preferred.

slides.heading: The waqf cases — where lesson 3-06's structure returns
body: When you STOP on a word ending in ر, the rā' becomes sākin, and the sākin rule applies to whatever is now in front of it. Five shapes cover everything she will meet.

A ر after a vowelled letter carrying a fatḥa or ḍamma: ٱلْأَبْتَرُ (108:3) → heavy. A ر after a SĀKIN letter which is itself after a fatḥa or ḍamma: ٱلْقَدْرِ (97:1) and وَٱلْعَصْرِ (103:1) → heavy. A ر after a YĀ' SĀKINAH: خَيْرٌ (97:3) → light. A ر after a sākin letter which is itself after a kasra: ٱلسِّحْرُ (10:81) → light. A ر that carried a kasra in waṣl: مُّقْتَدِرٍ (54:42) → light.
Then the sentence that carries the whole section: ٱلْقَدْرِ is light while you read on and heavy the moment you stop on it. The word did not change. Your stop did.

Read it both ways with her, twice each, until the two versions are audibly different and she can produce either one on request. Then say: this is exactly what happened with يُولَدْ in lesson 3-06. Same structure, different family. It has now come up twice, which makes it a general fact about recitation rather than a quirk of either rule.

The question to ask before every rā' at the end of a word is 'am I stopping here?' — and it has to be asked BEFORE the word, not during it. A decision made mid-word arrives too late to change the sound.

audio.cue: 97:1 — reference example, outside your memorized surahs, and the most useful word in the lesson. Reading ON: the ر has a kasra, so LIGHT. STOPPING: the kasra drops, the ر becomes sākin after a sākin د which is itself after a fatḥa, so HEAVY. Four readings: joined and stopped, twice each.
108:3 — stopping here, which is what you do at the end of the surah. The ر becomes sākin after a fatḥa, so HEAVY.
97:3 — reference example, outside your memorized surahs. Stopping: the ر follows a yā' sākinah, so LIGHT. The one waqf shape that goes the other way.

slides.heading: Drill 5 — the hamzat-waṣl test, and Drill 6 — the same word, both ways
slides.instructions: Drill 5: for each, ask 'does the kasra survive if I join?' out loud, and answer before reading. Drill 6: read each twice, joined and stopped, and make the two versions audibly different. Ask 'am I stopping here?' out loud before every single one — the habit is the point of the drill, not the words.

audio.cue: 89:28 — join it to the word before. The kasra vanishes, so it was never the rā's. HEAVY.
89:10 — the kasra is the ف's own and survives joining. LIGHT.
97:1 — joined: light. Stopped: heavy. Twice each, and they must sound different.
103:1 — joined: light. Stopped: heavy, because the sākin ص sits after a fatḥa.
97:3 — stopped: LIGHT, because a yā' sākinah is in front of the rā'. The shape that goes the other way.
108:3 — stopped: heavy. And this is a word she genuinely stops on, at the end of al-Kawthar.

slides.heading: Jawāz al-wajhayn — where both readings are correct
body: جَوَازُ الْوَجْهَيْنِ means literally 'the permissibility of the two faces': a small set of words where both a heavy and a light rā' are transmitted for Ḥafṣ, and either is right. Three cases, and that is all.

Case 1 — فِرْقٍ (26:63). A sākin rā' after an original kasra with an istiʿlāʾ letter, ق, following in the same word. That is exactly the shape of the five words above — but here the ق itself carries a KASRA, and a kasra'd istiʿlāʾ letter has its own downward pull, so it does not drag the rā' heavy with any force. Both readings transmitted; tarqīq is the more commonly preferred.

Say the thing this explains: this is why the exception list is exactly five and not six. فِرْقٍ has the same structure and a different answer. If she ever wonders whether the list is arbitrary, this is the proof that it is not.

Case 2 — مِصْرَ (10:87, 12:21) and ٱلْقِطْرِ (34:12), at WAQF only. In waṣl both are unambiguous: مِصْرَ has a fatḥa on the ر, so heavy; ٱلْقِطْرِ has a kasra, so light. The ambiguity exists only when you stop, because the rā' then becomes sākin and the letter before it is a sākin istiʿlāʾ letter. Preferred at waqf: tafkhīm for مِصْرَ, because the rā's original vowel was a fatḥa; tarqīq for ٱلْقِطْرِ, because its original vowel was a kasra.

Case 3 — words with a deleted yā', at waqf. Where the muṣḥaf's orthography has dropped a final yā', you may treat that yā' as present, in which case the rā' follows a yā' and is light, or as absent, in which case it is heavy. Tarqīq is generally preferred. يَسْرِ (89:4), فَأَسْرِ (11:81), نُذُرِ (54:16).

How to use this, in three instructions. Pick one wajh and HOLD it for the whole recitation — alternating within one sitting is not 'both permitted', it is inconsistency. Teach the preferred one as the default and the other as recognition only. And for cases 2 and 3 the ambiguity exists only at waqf; read on through and there is nothing to choose.

And the reason this section exists at all, said out loud: so that she stops treating a different reading as an error, and stops being rattled when a reciter she trusts does it the other way. This is a genuine, settled difference of transmission. Nobody is wrong.

audio.cue: 26:63 — reference example, outside your memorized surahs. Case 1. The ق carries a kasra, which weakens its pull. Both readings; tarqīq preferred. This is why the card is five words and not six.
10:87 — reference example, outside your memorized surahs. Case 2, at waqf only. Original vowel a fatḥa, so tafkhīm preferred when you stop.
34:12 — reference example, outside your memorized surahs. Case 2, at waqf only. Original vowel a kasra, so tarqīq preferred when you stop.
89:4 — reference example, outside your memorized surahs. Case 3, the deleted yā'. Tarqīq generally preferred.

slides.heading: Drill 7 — jawāz al-wajhayn, both faces, and Drill 8 — mixed, cold
slides.instructions: Drill 7: say each word twice, once each way, then pick one and keep it. The point of this drill is not performance — it is so that hearing the other version never rattles you. Drill 8: no warning, no grouping. Read and rule. Watch for صُدُورِ and وَٱسْتَغْفِرْهُ read heavy; those two are the diagnostic items.

audio.cue: 26:63 — light preferred. Say it heavy too, once, so it is never a shock.
113:2 — light, and it is a vowelled rā', so last lesson's rule.
97:1, STOPPING — heavy. Same word, second appearance in the drill on purpose.

slides.heading: Drill 9 — Sūrat al-Fīl, rā' patrol
slides.instructions: Read all five ayat and place every rā'. Six rā's in the surah proper, and every one of them is heavy — which makes it the cleanest page in the Qur'an for the sākin rule. Then Sūrat al-Falaq for contrast: بِرَبِّ heavy, then شَرِّ light four times over. Two short surahs, opposite answers. The basmalah at the head of each carries ٱلرَّحْمَٰنِ ٱلرَّحِيمِ, heavy both times, in every surah — count it separately or you will lose track.

audio.cue: 105:1 — heavy, fatḥa on the ر itself.
105:3 — heavy, fatḥa. And a heavy ط at the head of the word, from 3-07.
105:4 — heavy, fatḥa. Six for six: the whole surah is heavy.
113:1 — heavy. The only heavy rā' in al-Falaq proper.
113:2, 113:3, 113:4, 113:5 — light, four times. Opposite answer, four ayat later.

slides.translation: And He sent against them birds in flocks,

audio.cue: وَأَرْسَلَ — a sākin rā' after a fatḥa, so HEAVY. Say the vowel before the rā' out loud before you read the word. Then طَيْرًا: heavy ط from lesson 3-07, and a heavy rā' from its own fatḥa. Two heavy rā's in one short ayah, for two different reasons — one from the vowel before, one from its own.

slides.translation: striking them with stones of baked clay.

audio.cue: تَرْمِيهِم — a sākin rā' after a fatḥa, so HEAVY, and one tap, no roll: a sākin rā' gives the tongue more time to roll than a vowelled one, which is where the trill comes back. Then بِحِجَارَةٍ, heavy from its own fatḥa, with a heavy alif after it.

slides.translation: then glorify the praise of your Lord and seek His forgiveness. Indeed He is ever accepting of repentance.

audio.cue: وَٱسْتَغْفِرْهُ — the priority error of the lesson lives here. A sākin rā' after an ORIGINAL kasra, so LIGHT, and the heavy غ earlier in the word changes nothing because it is on the wrong side. Point at the page and ask which side the غ is on. Then رَبِّكَ in the same ayah: heavy, from its own fatḥa — two rā's, two rules, one ayah.

slides.translation: Indeed, it is the one who hates you who is cut off.

audio.cue: ٱلْأَبْتَرُ — and you stop here, because it is the end of the surah. The ḍamma drops, the rā' becomes sākin after a fatḥa, and it is HEAVY. Ask 'am I stopping here?' before the word rather than during it. Read it joined too, once, to hear that the ruling does not change in this particular shape — it is heavy either way, which makes it a gentle first waqf case.

slides.heading: Collapse the whole family back to two lines
body: She has now met roughly eight heavy conditions, six light ones, a five-word list and three ambiguous cases. Do not leave her holding all of it.
Write this and leave it up. A VOWELLED rā' takes its own vowel. A SĀKIN rā' takes the vowel before it — original kasras only, and a FOLLOWING istiʿlāʾ letter overrides.
Then: everything else is a footnote, and the five words are a card you keep in your pocket.

Say the bookkeeping fact out loud too, because it saves her worrying about a number. Some works give six conditions, some eight, some nine, and they all describe the identical recitation. They are grouping the same facts differently. Do not memorise a numbered list.

And name the one that will decay first: under continuous reading she will get the drill right and the recitation wrong. That is expected — eight conditions is more than working memory holds. The recovery is always the same two lines. Does the rā' have its own vowel? Then use it. No? Then look at the one before.

audio.cue: 114:5 — a vowelled rā'. Its own kasra decides. LIGHT.
110:3 — a sākin rā'. The vowel before decides, and it is an original kasra. LIGHT. Two different routes to the same answer, and she should be able to say which route she took.

slides.heading: Eight ways the sākin rā' goes wrong

mistakes.wrong: A heavy letter BEFORE the rā' pulling it heavy — وَٱسْتَغْفِرْهُ read with a heavy rā'.
mistakes.why: She has just learned that istiʿlāʾ letters affect the rā', and 'affect' has been heard as 'anywhere in the word'. Lesson 3-07 also spent a session on heaviness bleeding from neighbours, which primes exactly this. It is the priority error of the lesson.
mistakes.fix: 'Which side is the غ on?' Make her POINT at the page rather than answer from memory. Then the physical test: say both words slowly and notice where the tongue is at the moment the rā' happens.

mistakes.wrong: Treating a hamzat-waṣl kasra as a real one — ٱرْجِعِىٓ read light.
mistakes.why: The kasra is printed and looks like any other. Nothing on the page says it is temporary.
mistakes.fix: 'Join it to the word before. Where did the kasra go?' If it disappears, it was never the rā's.

mistakes.wrong: Extending the five-word list by analogy — any sākin rā' after a kasra read heavy because there is a heavy letter somewhere later in the word.
mistakes.why: She has learned the RULE behind the five words and is applying it, which is exactly what you told her not to do. It is an intelligent error and it should be named as one.
mistakes.fix: 'Is it on the card? Then it is light.' Five words, closed. And فِرْقٍ is the proof that the list is not arbitrary: same structure, different answer.

mistakes.wrong: Applying the waṣl ruling at waqf, or the reverse — ٱلْقَدْرِ read light when she stops on it, or heavy when she reads on.
mistakes.why: She decided the ruling when she saw the word rather than when she decided her stop. The decision has to come first, and mid-word is too late to change the sound.
mistakes.fix: 'Am I stopping here?' — asked BEFORE the word. Make it a spoken habit for a fortnight, exactly as with qalqalah kubrā in 3-06.

mistakes.wrong: Correcting someone who chose the other wajh — flagging a reciter's فِرْقٍ or مِصْرَ as a mistake.
mistakes.why: Everything else in the course has one right answer, so she has generalised that too.
mistakes.fix: 'Is that one of the three?' Both are transmitted for Ḥafṣ. Nobody is wrong.

mistakes.wrong: Switching wajh mid-recitation — the same word read two ways in one sitting.
mistakes.why: She has heard 'both are allowed' as 'it does not matter'.
mistakes.fix: 'Pick one and hold it. Both permitted is not the same as either at random.'

mistakes.wrong: Trilling, still — extra taps, especially on the heavy sākin rā's of تَرْمِيهِم and وَأَرْسَلَ.
mistakes.why: Unchanged from last lesson, and a sākin rā' gives the tongue more time to roll than a vowelled one does, because there is no vowel hurrying it off.
mistakes.fix: 'One tap. Press harder.' Record and count the contacts.

mistakes.wrong: Losing the whole family under load — correct answers in the drill and random answers in continuous reading.
mistakes.why: Eight conditions is more than working memory holds. This is expected rather than a failure, and saying so keeps her working.
mistakes.fix: Go back to the two lines. 'Does the rā' have its own vowel? Then use it. No? Then look at the one before.' Everything else is a footnote she can consult.

slides.heading: Two lines, one card, and one question asked before the word

audio.cue: 105:4 — a sākin rā' takes the vowel BEFORE it. Fatḥa, so heavy.
110:3 — original kasra before it, so LIGHT, and the غ is on the wrong side. Only a FOLLOWING istiʿlāʾ letter counts.
89:28 — the kasra must be original. This one belongs to a hamzat waṣl and vanishes when you join, so it does not count. Heavy.
6:7 · 9:107 · 9:122 · 78:21 · 89:14 — the card. All five outside your memorized surahs; reference examples, not hifz. Recognise, do not derive, do not extend.
97:1 — light while you read on, heavy the moment you stop. The word did not change; your stop did. Ask 'am I stopping here?' BEFORE the word.
26:63 — both readings transmitted, tarqīq preferred. Pick one wajh and hold it, and do not correct someone who chose the other.

slides.heading: Homework — 25–35 min/day, five days
tasks: Ten seconds — Drill 1. The two lines, out loud, before anything else.
Three minutes — Drill 2. Name the preceding vowel BEFORE reading the word. Every word, every time.
Two minutes — Drill 3. Which side is the heavy letter on? Point at it on the page.
One minute — Drill 4, the five-word card, twice a day. Recognise, do not derive. Then the sixth-that-isn't.
One minute — Drill 5. The hamzat-waṣl test: does the kasra survive if I join?
Three minutes — Drill 6. The same word joined and stopped. Ask 'am I stopping?' out loud first, every time.
One minute — Drill 7. Both faces, then pick one and hold it.
Three minutes — Drill 8, mixed cold, and Drill 9 — al-Fīl, then al-Falaq.
Hifz — Manzil (al-Fātiḥah), Sabqi (an-Nās whole and 113:1–113:2), then new Sabaq: al-Falaq 113:3, twenty to forty repetitions from the page.

Bring to the next session: the five-word card said from memory, and this answered — why is the list five words and not six? Next session is the lām of the Divine Name, which is the same idea as the rā' with ONE condition instead of eight.

108:3 — heavy when stopped, and heavy joined too.

drills.title: Drill 7 — jawāz al-wajhayn, both faces
drills.instructions: Twice each, once each way, then pick one and keep it. The point is that the other version never rattles you.

drills.title: Drill 8 — mixed, cold
drills.instructions: No warning, no grouping. Read and rule. صُدُورِ and وَٱسْتَغْفِرْهُ are the diagnostic items.

drills.title: Drill 9 — Sūrat al-Fīl, rā' patrol
drills.instructions: Six rā's in the surah proper, all heavy. Then al-Falaq for contrast. Count the basmalah separately.

audio.cue: 113:1 — heavy, and the only one in al-Falaq.

dailyChecklist: Drill 1 — the two lines, out loud, before anything else
Drill 2 — name the preceding vowel before reading the word
Drill 3 — which side is the heavy letter on? Point at it
Drill 4 — the five-word card, twice a day, then the sixth-that-isn't
Drill 5 — the hamzat-waṣl test: does the kasra survive if I join?
Drill 6 — the same word joined and stopped, asking 'am I stopping?' first
Drill 7 — both faces, then pick one and hold it
Drill 8 and Drill 9 — mixed cold, then al-Fīl and al-Falaq

script: Take her homework answer first: in صُدُورِ, why is the ر light when the ص before it is heavy? Because a rā' with its own vowel looks nowhere else. Today is what happens when it has no vowel of its own.

Write وَٱسْتَغْفِرْهُ (110:3) and قِرْطَاسٍ (6:7) side by side. Both have a sākin rā', both have a kasra before it, both have a heavy letter in the word. One is light and one is heavy, and reading them the same way means one of them is wrong.
Name the error before it happens: she will read وَٱسْتَغْفِرْهُ heavy because of the غ. The غ is a red herring — it comes BEFORE the rā', and only a FOLLOWING istiʿlāʾ letter counts.

Then the warning that is the real content of the lesson: this is where students start deriving. Do not. Condition 6 fires in exactly five words in the entire Qur'an. Learn to recognise five words and move on.

Check خُصَّ ضَغْطٍ قِظْ in the first two minutes. Every one of the five exception words is an exception because an istiʿlāʾ letter follows the rā'. If the seven letters are not automatic, this lesson will not stick.

Give the new baseline in one line, written next to last lesson's: a sākin rā' takes its ruling from the vowel BEFORE it. Then the whole family in two sentences, which she should be able to say from memory by the end of the unit.

Drill the plain cases before touching a qualifier, and lead from the surahs she is memorising. Spend the most time on وَٱسْتَغْفِرْهُ — it is in an-Naṣr, which she will memorise later in this unit, it is the best light sākin rā' she has in range, and the غ makes it a trap.

Qualifier 1: the kasra must be ORIGINAL. Give her the test as a sentence — 'if I join this word to the one before it, does the kasra survive?' ٱرْجِعِىٓ is heavy, and the kasra vanishes on joining. This is a small class and she does not need to hunt for them; she needs not to be surprised.
Flag now that this reverses next session: for the lām of the Divine Name every kasra counts, including connecting ones. Two rules, two answers, and she should not try to unify them.
Qualifier 2: give the five words as a CARD, not as a derivation. قِرْطَاسٍ 6:7 (ط) · وَإِرْصَادًا 9:107 (ص) · فِرْقَةٍ 9:122 (ق) · مِرْصَادًا 78:21 (ص) · لَبِٱلْمِرْصَادِ 89:14 (ص).

Say this to her in these words: all five of these are outside al-Fātiḥah and outside the last ten surahs. They are reference examples, not memorisation. You need to recognise them if one turns up on a page. You do not need to hunt for them and you do not need to derive them.

Two performance notes on the card: the alif after a heavy rā' is heavy, in قِرْطَاسٍ and مِرْصَادًا; and the istiʿlāʾ letter must follow in the SAME word — a heavy letter at the start of the next word does not reach back.

The waqf cases are where lesson 3-06's structure returns. Five shapes cover everything. Then the sentence that carries the section: ٱلْقَدْرِ is light while you read on and heavy the moment you stop. The word did not change; your stop did.

Read ٱلْقَدْرِ four times with her — joined and stopped, twice each — until the two versions are audibly different and she can produce either one on request. Then say explicitly that this is exactly what happened with يُولَدْ in 3-06: same structure, different family, second occurrence, so it is a general fact about recitation rather than a quirk.

The question before every word-final rā' is 'am I stopping here?', asked BEFORE the word rather than during it. A decision made mid-word arrives too late to change the sound. Make it a spoken habit for a fortnight.
Jawāz al-wajhayn exists so that she stops treating a different reading as an error. Three cases and no more: فِرْقٍ, then مِصْرَ and ٱلْقِطْرِ at waqf, then the deleted-yā' words at waqf.

فِرْقٍ also explains why the list is five and not six: the ق carries a kasra, which weakens its pull. Same structure, different answer. If she ever wonders whether the card is arbitrary, that is the proof it is not.

Three instructions for using jawāz: pick one wajh and hold it for the whole recitation; teach the preferred one as the default and the other as recognition only; and remember the ambiguity in cases 2 and 3 exists only at waqf.

Close by collapsing the family back to two lines and leaving them up. Then say the bookkeeping fact: some works give six conditions, some eight, some nine, and they all describe the identical recitation. Do not memorise a numbered list.
Hifz: Manzil (al-Fātiḥah), Sabqi (an-Nās whole and 113:1–113:2), then new Sabaq — al-Falaq 113:3, one ayah and the longest in the surah, twenty to forty repetitions from the page.

Three things from earlier lessons converge in 113:3, which makes it worth slowing down on. شَرِّ — light doubled rā', second of four; if it drifted heavy over the week, that is where the ten extra repetitions go. غَاسِقٍ — lesson 3-07's level 1 tafkhīm and the clearest inherited heavy alif she owns; the غ is heavy and the alif is heavy because of that and for no other reason. وَقَبَ — a light ب at the end, and a kubrā bounce if she stops on the ayah.
Set the homework question deliberately: why is the list five words and not six? She should arrive next session able to answer it with فِرْقٍ.

listenFor.item: A LIGHT sākin rā' after an original kasra, even when a heavy letter sits earlier in the word.
listenFor.commonMistake: وَٱسْتَغْفِرْهُ read with a heavy rā', pulled by the غ.
listenFor.whyItHappens: She has just learned that istiʿlāʾ letters affect the rā' and has heard 'affect' as 'anywhere in the word'. Lesson 3-07's session on heaviness bleeding from neighbours primes exactly this. It is the priority error of the lesson.
listenFor.correctionCue: Which side is the غ on? Make her point at the page. Then say both words slowly and notice where the tongue is at the moment the rā' happens.

listenFor.item: A hamzat-waṣl kasra correctly discounted — ٱرْجِعِىٓ read heavy.
listenFor.commonMistake: Reading it light because the kasra is printed and looks like any other.
listenFor.whyItHappens: Nothing on the page marks the kasra as temporary. Lesson 2-09 taught the hamzat waṣl as a sound that vanishes; nothing yet turned that into a ruling.
listenFor.correctionCue: Join it to the word before. Where did the kasra go? If it disappears, it was never the rā's.

listenFor.item: The five-word card treated as closed — recognised, not derived, not extended.
listenFor.commonMistake: Any sākin rā' after a kasra read heavy because there is a heavy letter somewhere later in the word.
listenFor.whyItHappens: She has learned the rule behind the five words and is applying it, which is exactly what she was told not to do. It is an intelligent error and naming it as intelligent keeps her from feeling caught out.
listenFor.correctionCue: Is it on the card? Then it is light. Five words, closed — and فِرْقٍ proves the card is not arbitrary.

listenFor.item: The waṣl/waqf decision made BEFORE the word — 'am I stopping here?' asked out loud.
listenFor.commonMistake: ٱلْقَدْرِ read light when she stops on it, or heavy when she reads on.
listenFor.whyItHappens: She decided the ruling when she saw the word rather than when she decided her stop. Mid-word is too late to change the sound. Same structure as qalqalah kubrā in 3-06, which is worth pointing out as a second occurrence rather than a coincidence.
listenFor.correctionCue: Ask the question before you reach the word, not while you are in it. Read it four times — joined and stopped, twice each — until both are on demand.

listenFor.item: A transmitted alternative recognised as an alternative rather than an error.
listenFor.commonMistake: Flagging a reciter's heavy فِرْقٍ or مِصْرَ as a mistake.
listenFor.whyItHappens: Everything else in the course has one right answer, so she has generalised that too. This is the first place the course says 'both, and nobody is wrong'.
listenFor.correctionCue: Is that one of the three? Both readings are transmitted for Ḥafṣ. Pick one wajh, hold it, and do not correct someone who chose the other.

listenFor.item: One wajh held consistently across a whole recitation.
listenFor.commonMistake: The same word read two ways in one sitting.
listenFor.whyItHappens: She has heard 'both are allowed' as 'it does not matter'. Permission to choose is not permission to vary.
listenFor.correctionCue: Pick one and hold it. Both permitted is not the same as either at random.

listenFor.item: One contact on a SĀKIN rā' — تَرْمِيهِم and وَأَرْسَلَ with no roll.
listenFor.makhraj: Tongue point 7, unchanged. Only the back of the tongue moves for weight.
listenFor.commonMistake: Trilling, which returns on sākin rā's even after it has been fixed on vowelled ones.
listenFor.whyItHappens: A sākin rā' gives the tongue more time to roll than a vowelled one, because there is no following vowel hurrying it off the ridge, and the tongue is already braced for a heavy letter.
listenFor.correctionCue: One tap. Press harder, not softer. Record it and count the contacts.

listenFor.item: The two lines surviving continuous reading, not only the drill.
listenFor.commonMistake: Correct answers word by word and random answers the moment she reads a whole surah.
listenFor.whyItHappens: Eight conditions is more than working memory holds under reading load. This is expected rather than a failure, and telling her so is part of the fix.
listenFor.correctionCue: Back to the two lines. Does the rā' have its own vowel? Then use it. No? Then look at the one before. Everything else is a footnote you can consult.

teacherNotes.homework: 25–35 min/day over five days. Daily: Drill 1, the two lines out loud before anything else (ten seconds); Drill 2, naming the preceding vowel before reading each word (three minutes); Drill 3, pointing at the istiʿlāʾ letter and saying 'before' or 'after' (two minutes); Drill 4, the five-word card twice a day, then the sixth-that-isn't (one minute); Drill 5, the hamzat-waṣl test (one minute); Drill 6, the same word joined and stopped, asking 'am I stopping?' out loud first (three minutes); Drill 7, both faces then picking one (one minute); Drill 8 mixed cold and Drill 9, al-Fīl then al-Falaq (three minutes). Hifz: Manzil (al-Fātiḥah), Sabqi (an-Nās whole plus 113:1–113:2), then new Sabaq al-Falaq 113:3, twenty to forty repetitions from the page — watching شَرِّ (light, second of four), غَاسِقٍ (level 1 tafkhīm and an inherited heavy alif) and وَقَبَ (a kubrā bounce if she stops). Bring to the next session: the five-word card said from memory, and this answered — why is the list five words and not six?
